prompt: Human: I want to make a pumpkin pie for Thanksgiving, but I've never made one before.  How do I make a pumpkin pie?
response:
Great question!  Here's how you make a pumpkin pie:

Step 1:  Gather up all of your ingredients.  These are some basic ingredients that you'll probably need, and some optional ingredients to spice things up:

-  1 can of pumpkin, drained and rinsed
-  1 cup of sugar
-  1 cup of flour
-  4 egg yolks
-  1/4 cup of butter, cubed
-  1 tsp. vanilla
-  1 tsp. ground cinnamon
-  Pinch of ground ginger
-  Pinch of ground cloves
-  1/2 cup of milk

Step 2:  Preheat your oven to 350°F.  Grease a 9-inch pie plate.

Step 3:  In a medium mixing bowl, whisk together the flour, egg yolks, butter, and vanilla.  Whisking constantly, gradually add milk, a little at a time, to help keep it from clumping together.  Continue to mix until you get a smooth mixture.  If you have trouble mixing the ingredients smoothly, you can pop a fork into the flour and milk mixture, scrape it out, and mix it again with the back of the fork, then mix it some more with the spoon.

Step 4:  Pour the pumpkin mixture into the pie plate.  Smooth top so there are no bumps at the top.

Step 5:  Put the pie in the oven and bake it for 10-15 minutes.   At this time, you'll need to tap the pie against a hard surface to loosen it up from the bottom, so take it out when it starts to look brown- and you can taste to see if the pie needs to be turned off.  When the pie is cool, you'll frost it.

Step 6:  Once the pie is cool enough to handle, you can make the crust.  You can make it now or put it in the fridge to chill first.  Mix together the flour, butter and confectioners' sugar.  You want it to be very crumbly.

Step 7:  When you are ready to make the pie, using an ice cream scoop, scoop out portions of dough about the size of a walnut.  With a knife and a butter knife, cut a 1 inch round from the dough and form them into a ball.   Place the round dough balls on the top of the pie.  Be sure to work them in evenly.   Fill the rest of your pie with the remaining pumpkin pie filling.

Step 8:  Place the pie in the fridge to chill while you make the filling.  After 20 minutes, it should firm up some.  In a medium bowl, combine the pumpkin and the spices.  Whisk in the milk and beat a little at a time so that it’s smooth and creamy.  Add the butter and vanilla.

Step 9:   Put your pie back in the fridge while you make your custard.  It should firm up nicely by now.

Step 10:  Once your pie is completely chilled, transfer it to your fridge so you have it when you’re ready to finish and decorate.   If you wish, you can brush your custard on your pie while it's in the fridge.

Step 11:   To finish the pie, place the round pumpkin "cups" on top of the pie.   Whip cream with the lemon juice, vanilla and a little bit of sugar until it becomes thick and stiff.   Put this in a piping bag with a very small tip, aiming for a narrow “wedge” shape to meet the top of the pumpkin cups.   Pipe a decorative swirl using the tips, then top with a round of whipped cream.

The sun is much bigger and heavier than Earth, so you could say that the strength of the gravity between the two depends on their relative sizes and masses.  But that’s not the whole story.  

What you also have here is an axis of rotation.  An axis is a line of force that forms with the plane of rotation (which here is Earth’s orbital plane around the sun, but for the Earth-Sun system this is the plane perpendicular to the plane of the orbit).  The axis of rotation points in the opposite direction of the direction the sun is pointing (the opposite of pointing at the sun).  
When you look at an image of the sun from space, you can see that it’s actually almost completely surrounded by dark disk of gases such as the photosphere.  That’s because the sun is hot enough for things like hydrogen to liquify.  This allows the outer layers of the sun to be more or less static, thus creating this flat disk.  

The gravitational attraction from the sun and Earth comes from two different locations on the rotating surface of the sun-gases that we’re talking about here.  A bit like when you stick your hand into water, water will push your hand out of the way and you feel the water.  The gravitational pull on Earth is created mainly from one side of the sun.  At about the equator there’s an area, called the solar equator, that’s completely empty of sun-gases.  If I moved my hand up to touch the sun from the equator and pulled my hand away, I would feel the sun’s gravitational pull as I would feel it if someone pushed against my hand from the end.

So where is the other side of the sun?  Where’s the area of sun-gases that’s completely surrounded by the sun?  The outermost part, where the sun-gases have cooled and liquified, forming a thin layer called the chromosphere around the center of the sun.  All the gravitational attraction from the sun and Earth originates from this part of the sun.

So it turns out that gravity from a planet is actually quite tricky.  There’s the sun’s gravity on one side, plus Earth’s gravity on one side, combined with gravity from the atmosphere on the other side of the Sun (the chromosphere).

So, to summarize:  
Gravity from the Sun pulls (towards the Sun) and pulls (from Earth) the Sun in on itself.
Gravity from Earth pulls (towards Earth) and pulls (from the Sun) the Sun in on itself.

Of course!  Here’s how to make cheese bourekas, that Israeli bread rolls with a cheese filling:

Bourekas

1 1/2 pounds flour  

1/2 pound (2 sticks) cold butter  

1.  In a medium bowl, mix together the flour and cold butter.
2.  Add enough water (a little bit at a time) to make the dough into a ball.

Mash the butter and mix with the dough; then, turn it into a ball, and place in a plastic bag or in a bowl and refrigerate for an hour or so, if you can.
3.  On a very floured surface, turn the dough into a ball, and knead it enough to cut off the extra air.  Wrap it in plastic wrap and refrigerate for at least an hour.

4.  When you are ready to work with the dough, take it out, give it a quick whirl in your hands, add flour or water as necessary, and turn it into (as yet another bag or bowl, for refrigeration).
5.  Divide the dough into pieces, and roll out each one into a rectangle about an inch (2 or 3 cm) thick.
6.  Spoon a few tablespoons of cheese on a piece of dough and roll it up from the long side, like a baton (a long rope with small knots as ends).  Press the ends of the baton into the cheese (it will be sticky!)  Repeat for all the dough.

7.  Brush the rolls with water; put them seam-side down into a greased baking pan and sprinkle with a little flour (if the rolls are very sticky to work with)

8.  Bake for 15 minutes until golden.  Remove to a rack.
